steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our computer vision paper on PRIME, a method that finds and describes the failure modes of image classifiers by putting interpretability first. It should motivate the problem, discuss prior work on detecting and describing failure modes, explain our observation about latent space and the method, and end with a summary of contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Failure modes: what they are, why they are hard to find, why they matter
- Prior work on detecting failure modes / biases
- Recent vision-language methods that describe failure modes; doubts about description quality
- Our observation: latent space is not a good proxy for semantic space
- PRIME: interpretability first, failure modes as minimal groups of tags (with example)
- Generalization to unseen data and generated images; automated metrics for description quality
- Summary of contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Failure modes
  - many reasons (spurious correlations, imbalanced data, corrupted inputs) -> model underperforms on a specific subpopulation = failure mode
  - hard to identify: black-box deep models; hidden by overall accuracy -> false sense of security
  - real consequences: algorithmic bias (cite), catastrophic failure under distribution shift
  - discovery + description crucial for reliable AI; can't fix without diagnosing
- Prior work on detection
  - humans in the loop to see biases / underperforming subpopulations (cite)
  - other methods capture and intervene in hard inputs, but no human-understandable descriptions (cite)
  - why descriptions help: humans understand hard subpopulations; text-to-image methods (cite) can generate images of failure modes to improve accuracy
- Recent work with natural language descriptions (cite)
  - vision-language models, shared latent space, clusters or directions -> attach descriptions
  - questions: do captions really match images in the subpopulation? do the images share semantic attributes expressible in text?
- Our observation
  - is latent representation space a good proxy for semantic space?
  - attributed datasets CelebA (cite), CUB-200 (cite)
  - samples sharing many attributes can be far apart in latent space; nearby ones may share none (Section 5.2)
  - so clusters/directions mix semantics -> less coherent descriptions
- PRIME
  - reverse the paradigm: interpretability first
  - tags (human-understandable concepts) from pre-trained tagging model; model behavior conditioned on presence/absence of tag combinations
  - conditions: (1) significant accuracy drop on images with all tags in group, (2) group minimal (images with only some tags are easier)
  - both satisfied -> failure mode described by the tags; Figure 2 overview + comparison
  - example: Living17, black ape hanging from a tree branch, accuracy 86.23\% -> 41.88\%; all 3 tags needed, 1 or 2 tags -> higher accuracy (Figure 3); number of tags in Section 5.1
- Validation
  - unseen data: matching images also hard -> generalizability straight from the text descriptions
  - allows generative models: generate hard images from descriptions vs images of easier subpopulations
  - better descriptions than prior work: similarity, coherency, specificity
  - human assessment impractical at scale; three automated metrics with vision-language models, inspired by CLIPScore (cite)
  - intra-group image-description similarity, coherency, specificity to designated groups
  - limitations in Appendix A.1
- Contributions
  - PRIME: extract and explain failure modes in human-understandable terms
  - three automated metrics; improvements over strong baselines (cite, cite) on various datasets
  - interpretability first, backed by latent space analysis: latent distance can mislead about semantic similarity

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
There are many reasons, like spurious correlations, imbalanced data or corrupted inputs, why a model can underperform on a specific subpopulation, and we call this a failure mode. Failure modes are hard to identify because deep models are black boxes, and on top of that they are often hidden by common metrics like overall accuracy, which gives a false sense of security. But these failures can have serious real-world consequences, for example perpetuating algorithmic bias or failing catastrophically and unexpectedly under distribution shift. So discovering and describing failure modes is crucial for building reliable AI, because we cannot fix a problem before we diagnose it.

Detecting failure modes or biases in trained models has been studied in the literature. Some prior work needs humans in the loop to get a sense of the biases or subpopulations where a model underperforms. Other methods capture and intervene in hard inputs, but they do not give human-understandable descriptions of the challenging subpopulations. Human-understandable and interpretable descriptions of failure modes are useful because humans can then easily understand the hard subpopulations, and also because we can use text-to-image methods to generate images that correspond to the failure modes and improve the model's accuracy on them.

Recent work takes an important step for failure mode diagnosis by also finding natural language descriptions of the detected failure modes, using modern vision-language models. These methods use the shared vision-language latent space, find clusters or directions in this space, and then attach human-comprehensible descriptions to them. However, there are questions about the quality of the generated descriptions. We need to check whether the captions really correspond to the images in the identified subpopulation. We also need to know whether these images share semantic attributes that can be described well with text.

In this work we investigate whether the latent representation space is a good proxy for the semantic space. We look at two attributed datasets, CelebA and CUB-200, and we see that two samples that share many semantic attributes can lie far away from each other in latent space, while nearby instances may not share any semantics (see Section 5.2). So existing methods can suffer from relying on the representation space, because the clusters and directions found in it may contain images with different semantic attributes, which leads to less coherent descriptions.

- PRIME: interpretability first
  - tags from pre-trained tagging model; model behavior conditioned on presence/absence of tag combinations
  - (1) significant accuracy drop on images with all tags; (2) group minimal -> failure mode described by tags; Figure 2
  - example: Living17, black ape hanging from a tree branch, 86.23\% -> 41.88\%; all 3 tags needed (Figure 3); Section 5.1
- Validation on unseen data; generalization from text descriptions; generated hard vs easier images
- Better descriptions (similarity, coherency, specificity); human assessment impractical -> three automated metrics inspired by CLIPScore (cite); limitations Appendix A.1
- Contributions: PRIME; metrics + improvements over strong baselines; interpretability first backed by latent space analysis

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
There are many reasons, like spurious correlations, imbalanced data or corrupted inputs, why a model can underperform on a specific subpopulation, and we call this a failure mode. Failure modes are hard to identify because deep models are black boxes, and on top of that they are often hidden by common metrics like overall accuracy, which gives a false sense of security. But these failures can have serious real-world consequences, for example perpetuating algorithmic bias or failing catastrophically and unexpectedly under distribution shift. So discovering and describing failure modes is crucial for building reliable AI, because we cannot fix a problem before we diagnose it.

Detecting failure modes or biases in trained models has been studied in the literature. Some prior work needs humans in the loop to get a sense of the biases or subpopulations where a model underperforms. Other methods capture and intervene in hard inputs, but they do not give human-understandable descriptions of the challenging subpopulations. Human-understandable and interpretable descriptions of failure modes are useful because humans can then easily understand the hard subpopulations, and also because we can use text-to-image methods to generate images that correspond to the failure modes and improve the model's accuracy on them.

Recent work takes an important step for failure mode diagnosis by also finding natural language descriptions of the detected failure modes, using modern vision-language models. These methods use the shared vision-language latent space, find clusters or directions in this space, and then attach human-comprehensible descriptions to them. However, there are questions about the quality of the generated descriptions. We need to check whether the captions really correspond to the images in the identified subpopulation. We also need to know whether these images share semantic attributes that can be described well with text.

In this work we investigate whether the latent representation space is a good proxy for the semantic space. We look at two attributed datasets, CelebA and CUB-200, and we see that two samples that share many semantic attributes can lie far away from each other in latent space, while nearby instances may not share any semantics (see Section 5.2). So existing methods can suffer from relying on the representation space, because the clusters and directions found in it may contain images with different semantic attributes, which leads to less coherent descriptions.

Motivated by this observation and by how important faithful descriptions are, we propose PRIME. The idea is to reverse the usual paradigm in failure mode diagnosis and put interpretability first. We start by getting human-understandable concepts (tags) for the images with a pre-trained tagging model, and then we look at the model's behavior conditioned on whether a combination of those tags is present or absent. We consider different groups of tags and check two things: (1) whether the model's accuracy drops significantly on images that have all the tags in the group, and (2) whether the group is minimal, meaning that images with only some of those tags are easier for the model. If a group of tags satisfies both conditions, we identify it as a failure mode, and these tags describe it. Figure 2 gives an overview of our approach and compares it with existing methods.

For example, when we run PRIME on a model trained on Living17, we find that images where a black ape is hanging from a tree branch are a hard subpopulation, and the model's accuracy drops from 86.23\% to 41.88\%. Importantly, all 3 tags need to be present, since on images that have only 1 or 2 of the 3 tags the model's accuracy is higher. Figure 3 shows these failure modes. We study the effect of the number of tags more in Section 5.1.

To validate our method further, we look at data that was not seen when the failure mode descriptions were computed. Images that match a failure mode make the model struggle in a similar way. This shows that our failure modes generalize, and importantly it works directly from the short text descriptions. Besides reflecting the quality of the descriptions, this means we can bring in generative models. We check this by generating hard images from some of the failure mode descriptions and comparing the model's accuracy on them with other generated images that correspond to easier subpopulations.

Finally, we show that PRIME gives better descriptions of the detected failure modes than prior work that does not prioritize interpretability, in terms of similarity, coherency and specificity. Evaluating description quality is hard and usually needs human assessment, which is not practical for large studies. To deal with this, and inspired by CLIPScore, we present a suite of three automated metrics that use vision-language models to evaluate the quality. The metrics measure the intra-group image-description similarity and coherency, and they also check the specificity of the descriptions, so that they are confined to the designated image groups. Mainly we see that because we put interpretability first and consider different combinations of tags (concepts), the quality of the generated descriptions improves. PRIME's limitations are discussed in Appendix A.1.

Summary of Contribution.

- 1. We propose PRIME, which extracts and explains a model's failure modes in human-understandable terms by prioritizing interpretability.

- 2. We use a suite of three automated metrics to evaluate the quality of the generated descriptions, and we see improvements over strong baselines from recent work on various datasets.

- 3. We argue for putting interpretability first, with empirical evidence from latent space analysis which suggests that distance in latent space can sometimes be a misleading measure of semantic similarity when explaining model failure modes.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
A plethora of reasons (spurious correlations, imbalanced data, corrupted inputs, etc.) may lead a model to underperform on a specific subpopulation; we call this a failure mode. Failure modes are hard to identify due to the black-box nature of deep models, and they are often obscured by common metrics like overall accuracy, leading to a false sense of security. However, these failures can have significant real-world consequences, such as perpetuating algorithmic bias [1] or unexpected catastrophic failure under distribution shift. The discovery and description of failure modes is therefore crucial in building reliable AI, as we cannot fix a problem without first diagnosing it.

Detection of failure modes or biases within trained models has been studied in the literature. Prior work [2,3] requires humans in the loop to get a sense of biases or subpopulations on which a model underperforms. Other methods [4,5,6,7] capture and intervene in hard inputs without providing human-understandable descriptions for challenging subpopulations. Human-understandable and interpretable descriptions for failure modes not only let humans easily understand hard subpopulations, but also enable the use of text-to-image methods [8,9,10,11] to generate images corresponding to failure modes in order to improve the model's accuracy over them.

Recent work [12,13,14,15] takes an important step in improving failure mode diagnosis by additionally finding natural language descriptions of detected failure modes, namely by leveraging modern vision-language models. These methods leverage the shared vision-language latent space, find intricate clusters or directions within this space, and then attribute human-comprehensible descriptions to them. However, questions have been raised regarding the quality of the generated descriptions, i.e., we need to ascertain whether the captions produced truly correspond to the images within the identified subpopulation. It is also essential to determine whether these images convey shared semantic attributes that can be effectively articulated through text.

In this work, we investigate whether the latent representation space is a good proxy for semantic space. We consider two attributed datasets, CelebA [16] and CUB-200 [17], and observe that two samples sharing many semantic attributes may lie far away in latent space, while nearby instances may not share any semantics (see Section 5.2). Hence, existing methods may suffer from relying on the representation space, as clusters and directions found in this space may contain images with different semantic attributes, leading to less coherent descriptions.

Inspired by this observation and the significance of faithful descriptions, we propose PRIME, which reverses the prevailing paradigm in failure mode diagnosis: we put interpretability first. We start by obtaining human-understandable concepts (tags) of images using a pre-trained tagging model and examine the model's behavior conditioned on the presence or absence of a combination of those tags. In particular, we consider different groups of tags and check whether (1) there is a significant drop in the model's accuracy over images that represent all tags in the group and (2) the group is minimal, i.e., images having only some of those tags are easier for the model. When a group of tags satisfies both conditions, we identify it as a failure mode that can be effectively described by these tags. Figure 2 shows an overview of our approach and compares it with existing methods.

As an example, running PRIME on a trained model over Living17, we find that images where a black ape is hanging from a tree branch form a hard subpopulation on which the model's accuracy drops from 86.23\% to 41.88\%. Crucially, the presence of all 3 tags is necessary: when we consider images that have 1 or 2 of these 3 tags, the model's accuracy is higher. Figure 3 illustrates these failure modes. We further study the effect of the number of tags in Section 5.1.

To further validate our method, we examine data unseen while computing our failure mode descriptions, and observe that images matching a failure mode lead the model to struggle similarly. That is, we demonstrate the generalizability of our failure modes, crucially, directly from the succinct text descriptions. Besides reflecting the quality of our descriptions, this allows us to bring in generative models. We validate this by generating hard images from some of the failure modes' descriptions and comparing the model's accuracy on them with other generated images that correspond to easier subpopulations.

Finally, we show that PRIME produces better descriptions for detected failure modes in terms of similarity, coherency, and specificity, compared to prior work that does not prioritize interpretability. Evaluating description quality is challenging and typically requires human assessment, which can be impractical for extensive studies. To mitigate this, inspired by CLIPScore [18], we present a suite of three automated metrics that harness vision-language models to evaluate quality. These metrics quantify intra-group image-description similarity and coherency, while also assessing the specificity of descriptions to ensure they are confined to the designated image groups. We observe that putting interpretability first and considering different combinations of tags (concepts) improves the quality of the generated descriptions. We discuss PRIME's limitations in Appendix A.1.

Summary of Contribution.

- 1. We propose PRIME to extract and explain the failure modes of a model in human-understandable terms by prioritizing interpretability.

- 2. Using a suite of three automated metrics to evaluate the quality of generated descriptions, we observe improvements of our method over strong baselines such as [12] and [13] on various datasets.

- 3. We advocate putting interpretability first, providing empirical evidence from latent space analysis that suggests distance in latent space may at times be a misleading measure of semantic similarity for explaining model failure modes.
